The question of whether Neanderthals interbred with modern humans has generated genuinely conflicting research outcomes. Several studies provide strong genomic evidence in favor of interbreeding: Neanderthal ancestry represents approximately 2% of non-African genomes [d1], all modern ethnic groups outside Africa carry traces of Neanderthal DNA [d6], and individuals today can have up to 1–4% Neanderthal DNA [d5]. Y chromosome and mitochondrial DNA analyses further suggest "strong gene flow" between the two groups, with interbreeding occurring as early as 270,000–100,000 years ago [d2], and modern human DNA has even been found in a Neanderthal woman from the Altai Mountains, indicating gene flow in both directions [d3][d4]. However, other research challenges these conclusions: Cambridge University researchers argued that a common ancestor approximately 500,000 years ago is sufficient to explain the shared DNA without any hybridization, calling interbreeding "very, very unlikely" [d8][d10]. Earlier studies based on mitochondrial DNA concluded that Neanderthals were a distinct species that "contributed nothing to the modern human gene pool" [d9][d11], and one model proposed that the absence of Neanderthal mtDNA in modern humans is best explained by intersterility or reduced fitness of hybrid offspring [d7]. The conflict reflects both the evolution of scientific methods over time and genuine disagreement about how to interpret shared genetic material—whether it reflects recent admixture or ancient common ancestry [d8][d10].
